When we watch a film, we see the actors.
But hundreds of people work behind the scenes.
The director is the boss on set.
He or she tells the actors how to play and decides how every scene should look.
The screenwriter writes the script: the story and every word the actors say.
The camera operator films the scenes.
Sometimes the same short scene is filmed twenty times from different angles!
The make-up artist can turn a young actor into an old man or a monster.
For some fantasy films make-up takes four or five hours every morning.
The costume designer makes the clothes.
In historical films every button must be right for the time.
The stunt person does the dangerous scenes instead of the actor: jumping from buildings, falling from horses or driving fast cars.
Without music, even the most exciting scene can feel boring.
At the end of every film there is a long list of names.
Next time, don't leave the cinema immediately.
Stay and read them: they are the people who made the magic.

Many people confuse England with the United Kingdom.
In fact, the UK is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Each one has its own capital and its own character.
Its capital, London, is famous for red double-decker buses, black taxis and the bobby, a friendly British police officer.
Many English people still enjoy high tea in the afternoon, with sandwiches, scones and cakes.
Scotland is famous for its rugged mountains, lakes called lochs and old castles.
Its capital is Edinburgh, but the biggest city is Glasgow.
The Scots invented golf, and there are hundreds of golf courses in the country.
Wales has a beautiful coastline with high cliffs and sandy beaches.
The Welsh have their own language, and road signs are written in Welsh and English.
Its capital, Belfast, is the city where the Titanic was built.
Near the coast you can see the Giant's Causeway, thousands of stone columns made by a volcano long ago.
Four countries, four flags, but one kingdom!

In 1873 the French writer Jules Verne wrote a famous novel,
Around the World in Eighty Days
Its hero, an English gentleman called Phileas Fogg, makes a bet with his friends.
He says he can travel around the whole world in just eighty days.
Fogg leaves London with his servant, Passepartout.
They travel by train and ship across Europe to Egypt, and then to India.
In India there is no railway in one part, so they ride an elephant through the jungle!
They continue to Hong Kong, Japan and across the Pacific Ocean to San Francisco.
Then they cross America by train.
On the way the train is attacked, and Passepartout bravely saves the passengers.
At last they sail across the Atlantic to Britain.
When Fogg arrives in London, he thinks he is one day late and has lost the bet.
But then he realises that, because he travelled east, he has gained a day.
He runs to his club just in time and wins!
Today you can fly around the world in less than two days.
But Fogg's journey shows that travel is about adventures and the people you meet, not only about speed.
